approaches.name: Posterior acetabular approach (Kocher-Langenbeck)
approaches.corridor: Gluteus maximus split followed by release and reflection of piriformis and the conjoined short external rotators

sources.title: Hip Posterior Approach Moore Or Southern

procedure_applications.condition: Posterior wall or posterior column exposure is required

positioning.text: Position prone or lateral; maintain hip extension and approximately 90 degrees of knee flexion to reduce sciatic-nerve tension.

setup.text: Prep the hemipelvis and entire limb to permit hip rotation, traction, and distal extension of the exposure.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the posterior superior iliac spine, greater trochanter, and lateral femoral shaft.

incision.text: Use a posterior curved incision directed toward the greater trochanter and then distally along the lateral femoral shaft.

superficial_interval.text: Incise iliotibial fascia distally and split gluteus maximus in line with its fibers, stopping before the first crossing neurovascular bundle.

deep_interval.text: Identify the sciatic nerve, then tag and release piriformis and the conjoined obturator internus–gemelli tendons lateral to their insertions for posterior-column exposure.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, iliotibial tract and gluteus maximus split, short external rotators, posterior capsule when required, then posterior wall and column.

structures_encountered.text: Piriformis, obturator internus, superior and inferior gemelli, sciatic nerve, greater and lesser sciatic notches, and posterior acetabular surface are sequentially encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: The sciatic nerve is at risk from direct pressure, stretching, misplaced retractors, and uncorrected tension during the exposure.
The medial femoral circumflex artery is endangered by release close to the short-external-rotator insertions and by needles passed during tendon repair.

danger_zones.text: Keep retractors out of the greater sciatic notch unless placed deliberately under direct protection; use the reflected external rotators as a cushion over the sciatic nerve.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid prolonged or forceful posterior retraction and repeatedly reassess sciatic-nerve freedom, particularly during reduction and fixation.

exposure.text: Directly exposes the posterior wall, posterior column, retroacetabular surface, greater and lesser sciatic notches, and selected dorsocranial articular surface.

limitations.text: Anterior-column and cranial anterior acetabular visualization is limited without an extensile maneuver such as trochanteric osteotomy.

extensions.text: A trochanteric osteotomy can add cranial and anterior exposure; selective quadratus femoris elevation adds caudal posterior-column exposure but increases vascular risk.

indications.text: Primary exposure for posterior-wall and posterior-column fractures and selected transverse or associated acetabular patterns requiring posterior reduction and fixation.

relative_contraindications.text: Use another or combined strategy when the principal reduction and fixation target cannot be visualized through the posterior corridor without unsafe extension.

implant_implications.text: Plan posterior-column and wall implant trajectories around the sciatic notches and confirm that clamps and screws remain extra-articular.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Arrange the table and equipment before positioning so obturator and iliac oblique views and AP pelvic imaging remain obtainable.

closure.text: Irrigate and debride nonviable tissue, then repair the released short external rotators, approximate gluteus maximus, and close iliotibial fascia and superficial layers.

complications.text: Major approach-related complications include sciatic neuropathy, heterotopic ossification, abductor or external-rotator dysfunction, femoral-head vascular injury, infection, and wound morbidity.

bailouts.text: If reduction cannot be confirmed or cranial/anterior visualization is inadequate, pause and add the planned extensile window rather than placing implants through unseen anatomy.

questions.question: How can positioning reduce sciatic-nerve tension during Kocher-Langenbeck exposure?
questions.answer: Maintain hip extension and approximately 90 degrees of knee flexion.

questions.question: Which tendons are reflected to expose the posterior column?
questions.answer: Piriformis and the conjoined obturator internus and gemelli tendons.

questions.question: Which vessel is protected by leaving a tendon stump lateral to the greater trochanter?
